contrasts.description: Compare oral close-mid /e/ with nasal /ɛ̃/. Listen to the whole vowel category: the difference is not just adding an n sound, and this is not the /ɛ–ɛ̃/ contrast.
contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French isolated forms. The nasal category is written broadly /ɛ̃/; actual quality varies by speaker. No final /m/, /n/ or /t/ is added. Keep oral /e/ distinct from /ɛ/.

contrasts.label: Rat or ré?
contrasts.description: Compare the open vowel /a/ with close-mid /e/ at the end of the word. The three frames keep their initial consonant unchanged within each pair.
contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French, explicitly selecting the dictionary /a/ variants for rat and the musical noun la. Their /ɑ/ variants are not silently relabelled. Ré and la name musical notes; lé is a less-frequent textile or wallpaper noun. Ces is the isolated lowercase determiner /se/, without liaison and not the acronym CES.

l1Notes.note: The /e/ target is one French vowel; avoid treating an English-style off-glide as required.
These sound categories may feel familiar; still use the recording rather than written letters to answer.

pairs.note: Select the independently documented /ʁa/ reading; /ʁɑ/ is also listed in TLFi and is not this target.

words.meaning: a full-width strip of fabric or wallpaper

pairs.note: La is the musical noun with selected /la/ reading; /lɑ/ is another dictionary variant. Preserve the accent in lé /le/, not le /lə/.
Ça is a pronoun and ces a determiner. Both are pronounced in isolation; do not supply a following noun, liaison /z/, or the uppercase acronym.

contrasts.dialectNote: Northern reference Metropolitan French citation forms with no final schwa. All three frames are one syllable; the final consonant is /l/ or /s/. Belle is the feminine form of beau; the selected ball sense of balle is not the older bale spelling.

l1Notes.note: French /a/ here is not a requirement to use the English vowel of cat.

contrasts.label: Jeûne or jeune?
contrasts.description: Compare close-mid /ø/ with open-mid /œ/ in the selected French readings. Both are rounded front vowels. This is a small, dialect-sensitive lexical contrast, separate from schwa /ə/.
contrasts.dialectNote: Use speakers who preserve the selected /ø–œ/ distinction. TLFi also lists veule /vœl/, which would merge that pair and must be rejected for this lesson. Jeûne and foehn have long-vowel dictionary transcriptions; broad IPA here does not assert equal duration or a pure-height experiment. Veule is literary; foehn is a specialist wind term; fun is a French borrowing. These are three distinct lexical frames, not three common beginner pairs.

l1Notes.note: Fun is the French word /fœn/ here, not an English /fʌn/ recording. The two French target vowels are both rounded.
Do not substitute /e/ or /o/, and do not treat the French schwa /ə/ as one of the two labels.

pairs.note: Preserve the accent in jeûne (fasting) versus jeune (young). Selected broad forms preserve /ø–œ/; older dictionary quantity is not an independent target here.
Use veule /vøl/. TLFi also permits /vœl/; that variant makes these words homophones and is not accepted for this contrast.

words.meaning: warm dry wind descending into Alpine valleys

pairs.note: Foehn is an established French wind noun; fun is the French informal adjective. This lexical frame is less familiar and cross-language synthesis is a particular listening-review risk.
